reviewed_diff: backend/orchestrator.py, backend/tests/test_orchestrator.py (pre-fix version, before findings below were addressed)

security_findings.finding: revert_transaction_endpoint returned a stale in-memory transaction.status to the client after revert_transaction's atomic claim lost a race (e.g. to purge_expired_delete_backups), contradicting the endpoint's own documented invariant that TransactionRevertError only ever means a physical-rollback failure.
security_findings.fix: backend/main.py: revert_transaction_endpoint now calls db.refresh(transaction) after catching TransactionRevertError before building the response.

security_findings.finding: purge_expired_delete_backups held its claim UPDATE uncommitted across shutil.rmtree, holding SQLite's whole-database RESERVED write lock for the duration of a potentially slow/unbounded filesystem delete — an app-wide availability risk once wired to a scheduler (any other concurrent write anywhere in the app would fail with 'database is locked').
security_findings.fix: backend/orchestrator.py: purge_expired_delete_backups now uses a three-state claim chain ('committed' -> 'purging' -> 'backup_purged', with a compensating 'purging' -> 'committed' rollback on rmtree failure) via _claim_transaction_status, with each step committed immediately so no write lock is held across shutil.rmtree.
security_findings.regression_test: backend/tests/test_orchestrator.py::test_revert_transaction_and_purge_expired_delete_backups_do_not_lose_the_race (updated to target the new claim timing)

security_findings.finding: _claim_transaction_status's session.execute() has no try/except around a possible raw sqlalchemy.exc.OperationalError under real SQLite lock contention (distinct from the deliberate rowcount==0 non-error outcome). It would propagate uncaught out of revert_transaction/purge_expired_delete_backups; main.py's endpoint only catches TransactionRevertError, so this becomes an unhandled 500 instead of the documented 200/409/404 contract.
security_findings.rationale: Not blocking for this low-priority task: purge_expired_delete_backups is not yet wired to any scheduler (no real concurrent contention exists today), and the project is a single-process desktop app where sustained lock contention is unlikely. Filed as a follow-up task.

security_findings.finding: The except OSError guard around shutil.rmtree in purge_expired_delete_backups is not exhaustive against every exception type an unusual filesystem could raise (e.g. platform-specific errors), which could leave the 'purging' claim state unresolved if an uncaught exception escapes.
security_findings.rationale: Same as above — low likelihood under current single-process deployment, orthogonal to the P0/P1 locking property this task targets. Filed as a follow-up task.

approved_points: The core compare-and-swap pattern (UPDATE ... WHERE id=? AND status=? + rowcount check) correctly works around SQLite's lack of with_for_update() support and is schema-free.
expire_on_commit toggling in _claim_transaction_status is correctly wrapped in try/finally.
The Saga #294/#295/#300 multi-root safety guard (only claim/purge if backup_dir exists under the caller's own allowed_root) is preserved unchanged and the new claim logic runs after that check.
The regression test correctly exercises both interleavings (revert-loses-to-purge, purge-loses-to-revert) using two independent Session objects against the same file-backed sqlite db.
overall_assessment: Two medium findings (endpoint stale-status, DB-wide lock held across a filesystem call) were fixed in-scope with regression tests. Two low findings (missing OperationalError handling, non-exhaustive rmtree exception guard) were judged non-blocking for this low-priority, not-yet-scheduled task and filed as a follow-up Saga task. The P0/P1 core locking guarantees from atdd.md are met.
